title: Mergers and Acquisitions (M&A) Strategy and Execution
subtitle: From strategic rationale and partner screening to valuation, deal documents, approvals and post-merger integration in Ethiopia
summary: Run an Ethiopian M&A deal end to end, from screening merger partners for a bank that missed the ETB 5 billion capital rule to negotiating the exchange ratio and delivering the integration plan.
audience: Investment banking analysts and associates, corporate development and strategy staff, bank M&A teams, deal leads, and legal and finance managers who work on acquisitions, mergers, strategic stakes and privatisations in Ethiopia. Completion of Financial Modelling and Valuation Level 1 or equivalent experience is expected.
objectives: Explain the strategic rationale and types of M&A and why many deals fail
Describe the deal process and the documents and approvals involved in Ethiopia
Perform accretion and dilution, synergy and purchase price allocation analysis
Run a sell-side or buy-side process, including auction design and bidder management
Structure consideration, protections and governance in an SPA and shareholder agreement
Plan post-merger integration and measure synergy delivery

runningCase.name: Bank A and Bank D
runningCase.text: Bank A is a fictional private Ethiopian bank with 140 branches, ETB 28 billion of assets and ETB 3.4 billion of paid-up capital, short of the ETB 5 billion minimum required of existing banks by 30 June 2026. Its board asks advisers to screen five mid-sized banks, Bank B to Bank F, as merger partners. Bank D, with ETB 55 billion of assets, ETB 5.8 billion of paid-up capital, a 16.2% capital ratio and little branch overlap, comes out first. The course then values the merger, sets the exchange ratio, structures the agreement, takes it through NBE and shareholder approval and plans the integration, ending in a negotiated merger simulation.

modules.title: Why companies merge and the Ethiopian deal landscape
modules.summary: Separate deals that create value from deals that only create size, then map where Ethiopian M&A is happening now: bank consolidation, foreign entry, privatisation and family successions.
objectives: Classify a deal as horizontal, vertical or conglomerate and name its strategic rationale
Explain how M&A creates value and the recurring reasons deals fail
Describe the forces driving Ethiopian deals after 2024: the ETB 5 billion bank capital rule, foreign entry, privatisation and succession
Frame the running case: Bank A's search for a merger partner

lessons.title: Horizontal, vertical and conglomerate deals
body: A horizontal deal joins two companies in the same business, such as two private banks or two flour mills. The prize is scale: a larger customer base over the same head office, IT platform and brand. A vertical deal joins companies at different stages of one value chain, such as a coffee exporter buying a washing station or a beverage maker buying its bottle supplier. The prize is control of supply, quality and margin.

A conglomerate deal joins unrelated businesses. Family groups in Ethiopia often grow this way, holding trading, manufacturing and real estate side by side. Conglomerate deals rarely produce operating synergies; their logic is usually access to capital, use of surplus cash, or spreading risk, and that logic must be tested hard because shareholders can usually diversify more cheaply on their own.

items.label: Horizontal
items.text: Same business, more scale: two private banks merging

items.label: Vertical
items.text: Up or down the value chain: an exporter buys a washing station

items.label: Conglomerate
items.text: Unrelated businesses under one owner: trading plus real estate

items.label: Market entry
items.text: Buying a local platform instead of building one: a foreign bank buys a stake

example.title: A vertical move in the coffee chain
example.text: Guji Highland Coffee Export PLC, owned by the Tadesse family, bought two washing stations near Hagere Mariam for ETB 85 million. Before the deal, a third of its export lots were downgraded for inconsistent processing. Within two seasons the share of lots graded at the top level rose, and the company could promise buyers traceable supply. The logic was quality and margin, not size.

lessons.tip: Before any numbers, write one sentence: the buyer will be worth more with the target because...

lessons.title: Growth, scale, capability and market entry
body: Most deals rest on one of four rationales. Growth: buying revenue faster than it can be built. Scale: spreading fixed costs, such as a core banking system or a national branch network, over more volume. Capability: buying skills, licences or technology the buyer lacks, such as a digital lending platform. Market entry: entering a new region, sector or country through a business that already has customers, staff and permits.

In Ethiopia a fifth rationale has become urgent: regulatory survival. A bank that cannot reach the minimum paid-up capital, or a microfinance institution below its capital floor, may merge because the alternative is losing its licence. That changes the negotiation: the weaker party has a deadline, and the stronger party knows it.
points: Growth: buy revenue and customers now
Scale: spread fixed costs over more volume
Capability: buy skills, licences or technology
Market entry: acquire a ready platform in a new market
Regulatory survival: meet capital or licensing rules by combining

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. MFI/36/2023, Minimum paid-up capital of microfinance institutions
regulation.text: A new microfinance licence requires at least Birr 75 million of paid-up capital fully paid in cash. Existing institutions below that level must reach it by January 2028 and keep a capital adequacy ratio of at least 12%. Institutions that fail the requirement may be put under receivership or merged, so merger is a recognised route to compliance.

lessons.title: Where value comes from and why many deals fail
body: A deal creates value for the buyer only if the value of the combined business exceeds the two stand-alone values by more than the premium paid and the cost of integration. Put simply, the buyer's gain is synergies minus premium minus integration cost. If the buyer pays away all the synergies as premium, the selling shareholders capture the value and the buyer's shareholders gain nothing for taking the risk.

Research on deals worldwide keeps finding that a large share of acquisitions fail to create value for the buyer's shareholders. The causes repeat: overpaying in a competitive auction, overestimating synergies, underestimating integration cost and time, culture clashes, losing key staff and customers during the transition, and weak due diligence that misses liabilities. Every one of these is a management choice, which is why disciplined process matters as much as strategy.

visual.caption: Pay away all the synergies and the buyer has taken the risk for nothing.

scenario.title: The trophy acquisition
scenario.situation: Koka Beverages PLC is bidding for Ziway Juice PLC in a three-bidder auction. Its team values Ziway at ETB 900 million alone and estimates synergies worth ETB 250 million. The CEO wants to win at any price because the deal would make Koka the market leader, and the latest bid needed to win is ETB 1,180 million.
scenario.question: What should the deal team advise?
options: Walk away or restructure: ETB 1,180 million exceeds stand-alone value plus all synergies
Bid ETB 1,180 million because market leadership is worth it
Bid ETB 1,250 million to make sure of winning
Ignore synergies and bid ETB 900 million
scenario.explain: The maximum a rational buyer can pay is stand-alone value plus synergies, here ETB 1,150 million, and even that hands all the synergies to the seller. Paying ETB 1,180 million destroys value for Koka's shareholders; size is not value.

lessons.title: Bank consolidation after the ETB 5 billion rule
body: The single biggest driver of Ethiopian M&A today is the bank capital rule. NBE's minimum paid-up capital directive (SBB/78/2021, reported) set ETB 5 billion for existing banks by 30 June 2026, and the licensing directive SBB/94/2025 applies the same Birr 5 billion floor to any new domestic bank, foreign subsidiary or foreign branch. Banks that could not raise enough from their own shareholders face three routes: a late rights issue, a strategic investor, or a merger.

At the same time, the risk-based capital adequacy directive SBB/95/2025 moves banks to Basel III style ratios with full compliance by 31 December 2026. A bank can meet the paid-up figure and still be short on risk-based capital if its loan book is heavy. So partner screening must look at both: paid-up capital and capital adequacy after the merger.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/95/2025, Risk-based capital adequacy
regulation.text: Banks must hold Common Equity Tier 1 of at least 7%, Tier 1 of at least 9% and total capital of at least 11% of risk-weighted assets, covering credit, market and operational risk. The directive took effect on 10 November 2025, with quarterly reporting from Q1 2026 and full compliance by 31 December 2026.

example.title: Bank A misses the deadline
example.text: Bank A, a fictional private bank with 140 branches and ETB 28 billion of assets, reached only ETB 3.4 billion of paid-up capital by 30 June 2026 despite two rights issues. Its board, chaired by Ato Mulugeta Haile, hired an advisory team to screen five mid-sized banks as merger partners. This is the running case for the course.

lessons.tip: In a capital-driven merger, model the combined bank's CET1, Tier 1 and total capital ratios, not only the paid-up total.

lessons.title: Foreign entry, privatisation and family successions
body: The Banking Business Proclamation No. 1360/2025 opened banking to foreign banks, which may enter as a subsidiary, a branch or by buying shares in a domestic bank. SBB/94/2025 caps foreign holdings in a domestic bank: up to 7% for a foreign individual, 10% for a foreign company, 40% for a strategic investor and 49% for all foreign holders together. A foreign strategic stake is therefore a minority deal with board influence, not a takeover, and must be structured that way.

Beyond banking, the Investment Proclamation No. 1180/2020 opens all sectors to foreign investors unless a regulation reserves them, and Investment Board Directive No. 1082/2025 opened most import, export, wholesale and retail trade. The state is selling stakes in public enterprises through its holding company, Ethiopian Investment Holdings, and the telecom sector has opened to a second operator and a public share offer. Finally, many family businesses founded in the 1990s now face succession, which creates management buyouts, minority growth deals and sales to strategic buyers.

items.text: Mergers driven by the ETB 5 billion capital floor and SBB/95/2025

items.label: Foreign stakes
items.text: Strategic investors up to 40%, all foreigners up to 49% of a domestic bank

items.label: Privatisation
items.text: Partial sales of state enterprises through Ethiopian Investment Holdings

items.label: Family succession
items.text: Second generation sells, buys out siblings or brings in a partner

items.label: Telecom and trade
items.text: Newly opened sectors attract foreign buyers of local platforms

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/94/2025, Licensing and renewal of banking business
regulation.text: Minimum paid-up capital is Birr 5 billion for a domestic bank, foreign bank subsidiary or foreign bank branch, paid in acceptable foreign currency for foreign subsidiaries and branches. Foreign nationals and foreign-owned Ethiopian organisations may together hold up to 49% of a domestic bank, with direct caps of 7% for an individual, 10% for a company and 40% for a strategic investor.

scenario.title: A foreign bank wants control
scenario.situation: A regional African bank tells Bank A's advisers it will invest USD 60 million for 51% of Bank A and full management control. Bank A is a domestic bank, not a foreign subsidiary.
scenario.question: How should the advisers respond?
options: Accept: control is the only way foreign banks will invest
Ask the NBE to waive the cap because Bank A missed its capital deadline
Split the 51% between the bank and two of its directors as individuals
Explain that 51% exceeds the 40% strategic investor cap; propose up to 40% with negotiated board seats and management rights
scenario.explain: SBB/94/2025 caps a strategic investor at 40% and all foreign holders at 49% of a domestic bank. Splitting the stake among related holders to dodge the cap would be treated as acting together; influence must come through the shareholder agreement and board rights.

lessons.title: The running case: screening partners for Bank A
body: Bank A's board has asked for a shortlist of merger partners among five mid-sized banks, called Bank B to Bank F. The advisers will screen them on strategic fit (branch footprint, customer segments, digital platform), financial strength (capital adequacy, asset quality, profitability) and deal feasibility (shareholder structure, governance, likely appetite).

The screen in this lesson is the first pass. Later modules take the chosen partner through valuation, the exchange ratio, the merger agreement, regulatory approval and integration. Keep the figures: they return in every module and in the final exam.

worked.title: Bank A: first screen of five candidates (ETB billions unless stated)

rows.label: Bank A (for reference): assets / paid-up capital / CAR / NPL
Bank B: assets / paid-up / CAR / NPL / branch overlap with A
Shortlist on strength and fit
rows.value: Bank D first, Bank B second

worked.note: E sits barely above the 11% minimum and would take on A's lower capital ratio; F and C bring weak asset quality. D adds the most capital per birr of risk with little branch overlap; B offers bigger cost savings but more integration work.

example.title: Why a complementary footprint can beat overlap
example.text: Bank D's branches are concentrated in Oromia and the south, while Bank A is strongest in Amhara region and Addis Ababa. Fewer branches can be closed, so cost synergies are smaller, but fewer customers are lost and the combined bank gains national reach. Bank B overlaps with A in 60 Addis Ababa locations: more savings, more disruption.

takeaways: Classify the deal and state its rationale in one sentence before modelling anything
The buyer gains only synergies minus premium minus integration cost; size alone is not value
Ethiopian bank M&A is driven by the ETB 5 billion paid-up rule and the SBB/95/2025 capital ratios
Foreign stakes in a domestic bank are capped at 40% per strategic investor and 49% in aggregate
Privatisation, newly opened sectors and family succession are the other big sources of Ethiopian deals

quiz.q: A coffee exporter buys the washing stations that supply it. What kind of deal is this?
quiz.explain: The target sits at an earlier stage of the same value chain, which makes it vertical.

quiz.q: Which expression gives the buyer's gain from an acquisition?
options: Synergies minus premium minus integration cost
quiz.explain: The buyer keeps only the synergies it does not pay away as premium or spend on integration.

quiz.q: Under SBB/94/2025, the largest stake a single foreign strategic investor may hold in a domestic bank is:
quiz.explain: Strategic investors may hold up to 40%; 49% is the aggregate foreign cap.

quiz.q: Which minimum total capital ratio does SBB/95/2025 set?
quiz.explain: Total capital must be at least 11% of risk-weighted assets, with CET1 at 7% and Tier 1 at 9%.

quiz.q: Why did Bank E fall down Bank A's shortlist despite being the largest candidate?
options: Its branches do not overlap with Bank A
It has too much paid-up capital
Its capital ratio of 11.4% leaves almost no room above the minimum after absorbing Bank A
quiz.explain: Combining with a bank that already sits near the 11% floor risks a merged ratio below the minimum.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a common reason acquisitions fail?
options: Careful due diligence that finds hidden liabilities
Losing key staff and customers in transition
quiz.explain: Finding liabilities in due diligence protects the buyer; missing them is the failure.

modules.title: The deal process, approvals and basic deal maths
modules.summary: Run a deal from screening to closing, line up the Ethiopian approvals in the right order, and test a merger with synergy, accretion and dilution, and purchase price allocation.
objectives: Sequence the deal process from strategy and screening to signing and closing, with the documents at each step
Map the approvals an Ethiopian deal may need: competition authority, NBE, ECMA, Ethiopian Investment Commission and sector regulators
Calculate accretion or dilution and the synergies needed to break even
Explain purchase price allocation and goodwill in simple terms
Write a partner screening memo for Bank A

lessons.title: From strategy to closing
body: Every well-run deal follows the same spine. The buyer sets a strategy and screening criteria, builds a long list, narrows it to a short list and makes a discreet approach. Both sides sign a non-disclosure agreement (NDA), and the seller's adviser shares a short teaser and then an information memorandum (IM). Bidders send indicative, non-binding offers; the best are admitted to due diligence; they then submit binding offers with a marked-up sale and purchase agreement (SPA).

Signing commits both parties subject to conditions precedent, usually regulatory approvals and shareholder resolutions. Closing, which may come months later in Ethiopia, is when the shares and the money change hands. The gap between signing and closing is where deals break, so the SPA must say what happens if approvals are delayed or the target's business deteriorates.

example.title: A process that skipped the NDA
example.text: The owner of Bahir Dar Textile PLC, Wro. Almaz Kebede, shared her full customer list with a prospective buyer at a first meeting without an NDA. The buyer withdrew a month later and two of her largest garment customers began receiving offers from the buyer's own mill. A signed NDA with a non-solicitation clause would have given her a remedy.

lessons.title: The Ethiopian approvals map
body: Ethiopian deals often need several approvals, and the slowest one sets the timetable. A merger above the thresholds of the trade competition law must be notified to the Ethiopian Trade Competition and Consumers Protection Authority, which may clear it, clear it with conditions or block it (Proclamation No. 813/2013, as cited in the course specification; confirm the current text and thresholds). A deal involving a bank needs NBE approval, including approval of every person who will hold 2% or more of the bank under SBB/89/2024.

A foreign buyer needs an investment permit from the Ethiopian Investment Commission and must meet the Investment Proclamation's minimum capital and sector rules. Deals involving listed securities or capital market service providers bring in ECMA, and sector regulators such as the telecom or insurance supervisor may add their own approvals. The Commercial Code No. 1243/2021 sets the company law steps: board proposals, general meeting resolutions, creditor protection and registration of the change.

items.label: Competition authority
items.text: Merger notification and clearance above the thresholds

items.label: NBE
items.text: Bank mergers, significant shareholders (2% or more), directors and CEO

items.label: ECMA
items.text: Listed securities, public offers, capital market service providers

items.label: Investment Commission
items.text: Foreign investor permit and sector eligibility

items.label: Company law steps
items.text: Board and general meeting resolutions, creditors, registration

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/89/2024, Persons with significant influence
regulation.text: The NBE must approve influential shareholders, meaning those holding 2% or more of a bank, as well as directors, the CEO and senior executives. In a bank merger, every shareholder who will reach 2% of the combined bank needs approval before closing, so the shareholder register must be mapped early.

scenario.title: Which approval first?
scenario.situation: Bank D and Bank A have agreed heads of terms. Bank D's legal head proposes holding both banks' extraordinary general meetings next month and only then approaching the NBE, because 'there is no point asking the regulator before shareholders agree'.
scenario.question: What is the better sequence?
options: Consult the NBE informally first, map 2% holders and fit-and-proper needs, then seek shareholder approval on terms the regulator is likely to accept
Close the merger first and notify the NBE afterwards
Skip the competition authority because banks are regulated by the NBE
scenario.explain: Shareholders asked to vote on terms the NBE later rejects would have to vote again. Early regulatory consultation, a shareholder map and a competition filing check reduce the risk of a failed or repeated process.

lessons.title: Estimating synergies
body: Synergies come in two kinds. Cost synergies, such as closing overlapping branches, merging head offices and running one core banking system, are within management's control and are the more reliable. Revenue synergies, such as cross-selling trade finance to the other bank's customers, depend on customers' choices and are usually discounted heavily or left out of the price.

Every synergy needs four things: a source, a run-rate amount, a phasing over time and a one-off cost to achieve it. A branch closure saves rent and staff costs each year, but it costs severance, lease exits and system work up front, and it may lose some deposits. Net the costs and the leakage before you count the benefit.

worked.title: Bank A and Bank D: run-rate cost synergies (ETB millions a year)

rows.label: Close 35 overlapping branches at about ETB 6 million each
One core banking system, licences and data centre
Less expected deposit attrition cost from closures
One-off integration cost over two years
After-tax run-rate at an assumed 30% tax rate

worked.note: The deal must earn back ETB 450 million of integration cost before synergies add value; phasing matters as much as the run-rate.

lessons.tip: Treat revenue synergies as upside to the case, not as a reason to pay a higher price.

lessons.title: Accretion and dilution
body: In a share-for-share merger, the buyer issues new shares to the target's shareholders. The question is whether earnings per share (EPS) of the combined company are higher (accretive) or lower (dilutive) than the buyer's EPS alone. Combined EPS equals combined net profit, including after-tax synergies, divided by the buyer's existing shares plus the new shares issued.

Dilution is not automatically bad: a deal can be dilutive in year one and still create value if synergies build up later or if the buyer gains capital and growth. But the board must know the number, and the analyst should always compute the synergies needed to break even.

parts.label: Buyer profit + target profit + after-tax synergies

visual.caption: Compare with the buyer's stand-alone EPS: higher is accretive, lower is dilutive.

worked.title: Bank D issues shares for Bank A at book value (shares in millions, ETB millions)

rows.label: Bank D: net profit / shares / EPS
Book value per share: A (4,600 / 3.40) and D (8,700 / 5.80)
Combined EPS with ETB 210 million after-tax synergies (2,210 / 8.87)
After-tax synergies needed to break even (250 x 8.87 minus 2,000)

worked.note: At book value the deal is close to neutral only once synergies are fully delivered. Any premium to Bank A makes it more dilutive.

lessons.title: Purchase price allocation and goodwill
body: After an acquisition the buyer must record the target's assets and liabilities at fair value, not at the target's book value. The difference between the price paid and the fair value of the net identifiable assets is goodwill. Ethiopian banks and large companies report under IFRS, whose business combination standard sets this method.

For a bank, the biggest adjustments are usually to the loan book (fair value below book if credit risk is under-provided), premises (often above book after years of inflation) and new intangibles such as the value of core deposits. Goodwill matters for bank capital because Basel III style rules typically deduct goodwill and intangibles from Common Equity Tier 1, so a high price can reduce the capital the merger was meant to build.

worked.title: Bank A: illustrative purchase price allocation (ETB millions)

rows.label: Consideration: 3.07 million D shares at an agreed fair value of Birr 1,800
Deferred tax on net adjustments (30% of 130)
Fair value of net identifiable assets

worked.note: If goodwill is deducted from CET1, about ETB 0.8 billion of the merged bank's capital will not count toward its ratios.

example.title: The revaluation surprise
example.text: When Hawassa Dairy PLC was bought by a larger food group, its factory land use right and building in the city had been carried at cost since 2009. Valuers placed the premises at more than three times book value. The higher fair value cut goodwill sharply but raised future depreciation, which lowered reported profit in the first years after the deal.

lessons.title: Capstone: the partner screening memo
body: The first capstone is a two-page memo to Bank A's board. It states the objective (meet the capital rule and build a stronger bank), the screening criteria and weights, the results for Banks B to F, the recommended shortlist with reasons, the main risks and the next steps. It is a recommendation, so it ends with a clear request: approval to approach Bank D first and Bank B as an alternative.

A strong memo shows the numbers but leads with judgment. It explains why the largest bank is not automatically the best partner, shows the post-merger capital ratio, and flags what the advisers do not yet know, such as each candidate's shareholder appetite and the true quality of its loan book.
points: Objective and constraints, including the capital deadline
Criteria and weights: capital, asset quality, fit, feasibility
Scores for each candidate and the shortlist
Indicative merged capital and EPS effect
Key risks and unknowns
Decision requested and next steps

scenario.title: A board member's favourite
scenario.situation: A Bank A director, Ato Bekele Gemechu, presses the advisers to put Bank F at the top of the shortlist because its chairman is a long-standing business contact. Bank F has the weakest NPL ratio of the five at 9.6% and large exposures to companies linked to its own shareholders.
scenario.question: How should the memo handle this?
options: Rank Bank F first to keep the director on side
Leave Bank F out of the memo entirely
Score Bank F on the same criteria, show why it ranks low, and note the director's interest so the board can manage the conflict
Rank all five equally to avoid conflict
scenario.explain: The board needs an objective screen. Applying the same criteria and disclosing a director's relationship lets the board decide properly and protects the advisers' independence.

takeaways: The deal spine runs from strategy to closing; the signing to closing gap is where deals break
Map every approval early: competition authority, NBE (including 2% shareholders), Investment Commission, ECMA and sector regulators
Count cost synergies net of one-off costs and leakage; treat revenue synergies as upside
Always compute accretion or dilution and the synergies needed to break even
Goodwill from purchase price allocation can reduce a merged bank's CET1

quiz.q: At which stage do bidders normally submit a marked-up SPA?
options: With binding offers after due diligence
quiz.explain: Binding offers come after due diligence and include the bidder's mark-up of the SPA.

quiz.q: Under SBB/89/2024, which shareholders of a merged bank need NBE approval?
options: None, if the merger is approved
quiz.explain: SBB/89/2024 treats holders of 2% or more as influential, and they need NBE approval.

quiz.q: Bank D's EPS is Birr 250. After the merger, combined EPS is Birr 240. The deal is:
quiz.explain: (240 minus 250) / 250 = minus 4%, so the deal is 4% dilutive.

quiz.q: Which synergy is generally most reliable?
options: New products the target may launch
quiz.explain: Cost synergies within management's control are more reliable than revenue synergies.

quiz.q: Price paid is ETB 2,000 million; fair value of net identifiable assets is ETB 1,650 million. Goodwill is:
quiz.explain: Goodwill equals price minus fair value of net identifiable assets: 2,000 minus 1,650.

quiz.q: Why can a high acquisition price weaken a merged bank's capital position?
options: Goodwill must be paid in foreign currency
Goodwill is usually deducted from CET1
quiz.explain: Basel III style rules typically deduct goodwill and intangibles from CET1, so more goodwill means less counted capital.

modules.title: Running the process and valuing the deal
modules.summary: Design a buy-side or sell-side process, manage bidders and data rooms, and value a target with control premium, synergy value, a merger model and a share-for-share exchange ratio.
objectives: Choose between an auction and a bilateral negotiation and design the process letter and data room
Manage bidders to keep competitive tension without losing credibility
Value control and synergies, and set a walk-away price
Build and negotiate a share-for-share exchange ratio for Bank A and Bank D

lessons.title: Mandates, long lists and the choice of process
body: A sell-side mandate letter sets the adviser's scope, exclusivity, fees (usually a retainer plus a success fee) and conflicts rules. A buy-side mandate adds the client's screening criteria and a cap on the price the adviser may indicate. The long list for a sale includes strategic buyers, financial investors and, since 2024, foreign entrants into newly opened sectors.

An auction maximises price when several credible bidders exist and the business can be described well in an IM. A bilateral negotiation suits a sensitive deal with one obvious partner, such as a bank merger where confidentiality protects deposits and staff. Many Ethiopian deals use a hybrid: a quiet approach to two or three parties, then a short competitive phase.

left.title: Auction
items: Best when several credible bidders exist
Process letter fixes rules and deadlines
Risk of leaks and a failed public sale

right.title: Bilateral
items: Best for sensitive or regulated deals
Seller needs an outside view of value

regulation.source: Capital Market Proclamation No. 1248/2021 and ECMA Directive No. 980/2024, Licensing of capital market service providers
regulation.text: Firms that act as investment banks or advisers in the capital market must be licensed by ECMA, which sets 15 licence categories with minimum capital from Birr 100,000 for an individual adviser to Birr 100 million for a bank-group investment bank, a 40% liquid asset requirement and annual renewal. No ECMA takeover directive for listed companies was confirmed in the course materials, so check ECMA notices before any deal involving an ESX-listed company.

example.title: A hybrid process for a family business
example.text: The three Tadesse siblings who own Guji Highland Coffee Export PLC wanted to sell 60% when their father retired. Their adviser, Hanna Girma, approached two foreign coffee traders and one Ethiopian agro-industrial group under NDAs, then ran a six-week second round. The competing interest raised the best offer from ETB 640 million to ETB 760 million without a public sale that might have unsettled their buyers.

lessons.title: Process letters, data rooms and bidder management
body: A process letter tells bidders what to submit and when: price and the basis for it (enterprise or equity value, cash-free and debt-free or not), financing, conditions, approvals needed, and a mark-up of the SPA in round two. Precise instructions make bids comparable. The data room, now almost always virtual, holds documents in a structured index, with tiered access so that the most sensitive items, such as customer lists or staff salaries, open only to the final bidder.

Bidder management is about keeping tension credible. Give every bidder the same information at the same time, answer questions through one channel, keep deadlines unless there is a real reason to move them, and never invent a rival bid. Ethiopian records are often incomplete, so prepare a vendor fact book in advance and reconcile management accounts to audited statements before bidders find the gaps.
points: Same information to all bidders at the same time
One channel for questions, with a log
Tiered data room access for sensitive items
Firm deadlines, moved only for a real reason
No invented rival bids: credibility is the adviser's capital

scenario.title: A bidder asks for exclusivity
scenario.situation: In the Guji Highland sale, the agro-industrial group offers ETB 720 million if it gets four weeks of exclusivity now, before second-round bids are due in ten days. The two foreign traders have indicated ETB 680 million and ETB 700 million and are still in diligence.
scenario.question: What should the sell-side adviser recommend?
options: Grant exclusivity immediately because it is the highest number
Tell the foreign traders a rival has bid ETB 800 million
Keep the timetable: tell the group that exclusivity follows the second round and invite it to put its best binding offer in by the deadline
End the process and sign with the group without an SPA mark-up
scenario.explain: Granting exclusivity now gives up competitive tension for a small premium on a non-binding number. Holding to the timetable keeps all three bidders honest; inventing a bid would destroy the adviser's credibility.

lessons.title: Control premium and synergy value
body: A buyer of control can change strategy, management, dividends and capital structure, so a controlling stake is usually worth more per share than a minority stake. The control premium a buyer can afford, however, comes from what it can do differently: the synergies and improvements it alone can deliver. Paying a premium for control without a plan to use it simply transfers value to the seller.

Value synergies like any cash flow: forecast their phasing, deduct integration costs, tax them, and discount them at a rate that reflects their risk, which is usually at least the target's cost of equity. In high-rate Ethiopia, with the National Bank Rate at 16% since July 2026, discount rates are high and synergies that arrive late are worth much less than the run-rate suggests.

worked.title: Bank A and Bank D: present value of synergies (ETB millions, 22% cost of equity)

rows.label: Year 1: after-tax synergies 63 (30% of run-rate) less after-tax integration cost 200
Year 2: after-tax synergies 147 (70%) less after-tax integration cost 115
Present value of year 3 onward (210 / 0.22, discounted two years)

worked.note: The synergies are worth about ETB 550 million today, much less than a simple multiple of the ETB 300 million run-rate would suggest.

visual.caption: Integration costs come first and benefits later, which is why phasing drives value.

lessons.title: Merger model and walk-away price
body: A merger model combines the two companies' forecasts, adds synergies and integration costs, applies the financing (cash, new shares or debt) and shows combined EPS, capital ratios and ownership for each year. Its most useful output in negotiation is the maximum price: the price at which the buyer's shareholders are no worse off than without the deal.

Set the walk-away price before talks start and write it down. Maximum price equals the target's stand-alone value plus the present value of synergies the buyer is willing to share, less integration costs not already deducted. The negotiating range lies between the seller's minimum (its stand-alone value or best alternative) and the buyer's maximum; the deal team's job is to close as near the bottom of that range as possible.

parts.label: PV of synergies (net of integration cost)

visual.caption: Paying the maximum hands all the synergies to the seller; the target price is well below it.

scenario.title: Sharing the synergies
scenario.situation: Koka Beverages values Ziway Juice at ETB 900 million alone and net synergies at ETB 250 million. Ziway's owners have a firm offer from a financial investor at ETB 950 million.
scenario.question: Within which range should Koka negotiate?
options: ETB 950 to 1,150 million, aiming near the bottom
Exactly ETB 900 million, take it or leave it
scenario.explain: The seller will not accept less than its best alternative of ETB 950 million, and Koka should not pay more than ETB 1,150 million. Closing near ETB 950 to 1,000 million keeps most synergies for Koka's shareholders.

lessons.title: Share-for-share exchange ratios
body: In a merger of two unlisted Ethiopian banks there is no market price to anchor the exchange ratio, so the parties negotiate it from book value, adjusted net asset value, earnings, dividend capacity and a valuation of each bank's franchise. The ratio decides who owns what share of the combined bank, and therefore who controls the board and who captures the synergies.

Each point of premium in the ratio transfers value from the buyer's shareholders to the target's. In the Bank A and Bank D case, a 10% premium to the book value ratio gives Bank A's shareholders roughly the whole present value of the synergies. Bank D's negotiators should therefore trade any premium for something of value, such as a lower number of Bank A board seats or Bank A shareholders bearing a loan book adjustment.

worked.title: Bank A and Bank D: exchange ratio options (shares in millions)

rows.label: Book value ratio
rows.value: 0.902; A holders own 34.6% of the combined bank

rows.label: Earnings ratio (A EPS Birr 162 / D EPS Birr 250)
Extra D shares from the premium (3.37 minus 3.07)
Value of extra shares at Birr 1,800
PV of synergies from the earlier calculation
Combined EPS with full synergies at the premium ratio (2,210 / 9.17)

worked.note: A 10% premium gives Bank A's holders essentially all the synergies; Bank D should concede it only for something valuable in return.

example.title: Negotiating on earnings, not only book
example.text: In a merger of two fictional microfinance institutions in Sidama region, the larger one, with a far higher return on equity, insisted that the ratio reflect earnings as well as book value. The parties settled on a weighted average: 60% book value ratio and 40% earnings ratio. Both boards could explain the formula to their shareholders, which helped win the general meeting votes.

takeaways: Choose auction, bilateral or hybrid to fit the number of credible buyers and the sensitivity of the deal
Keep bidder management fair and credible: same information, firm deadlines, no invented bids
Value synergies as risky cash flows net of integration cost; late synergies are worth little at Ethiopian rates
Set the walk-away price before talks and negotiate near the seller's best alternative
In a share-for-share deal, every point of exchange ratio premium transfers synergy value to the target's holders

quiz.q: When is a bilateral negotiation usually preferred to an auction?
options: When the deal is sensitive and one partner is clearly best
When the seller wants the highest price at any cost
When the business is easy to describe
quiz.explain: Bilateral deals suit sensitive situations such as bank mergers with one obvious partner.

quiz.q: Why should a process letter specify whether bids are cash-free and debt-free?
quiz.explain: Bids on different bases cannot be compared; the letter sets a common basis.

quiz.q: A target's stand-alone value is ETB 600 million and net synergies are worth ETB 150 million. The buyer's maximum price is:
quiz.explain: Maximum price equals stand-alone value plus the value of synergies: 600 plus 150.

quiz.q: Why are late-arriving synergies worth much less in Ethiopia today?
options: High discount rates reduce the present value of distant cash flows
Synergies must be paid in dollars
quiz.explain: With policy rates around 16% and higher costs of equity, distant cash flows are discounted heavily.

quiz.q: In the Bank A and Bank D case, what does a 10% premium on the book value exchange ratio do?
options: Gives Bank A's holders about all the PV of synergies
quiz.explain: The extra shares are worth about ETB 552 million, almost the full PV of synergies.

quiz.q: What should a sell-side adviser never do to keep competitive tension?
options: Give all bidders the same information
quiz.explain: Inventing a bid is dishonest and destroys the adviser's credibility if discovered.

modules.title: Structuring the deal and the legal documents
modules.summary: Choose between asset and share deals, cash and shares, earn-outs, escrow and locked box or completion accounts, then turn the deal into a term sheet, SPA and shareholder agreement that protect each side.
objectives: Compare asset and share deals and the Ethiopian tax and transfer issues of each
Structure consideration with cash, shares, deferred payment, earn-outs and escrow
Choose between a locked box and completion accounts and compute the price adjustment
Draft the key protections: representations and warranties, indemnities, MAC clause and conditions precedent
Design governance terms in a shareholder agreement for a minority strategic investor

lessons.title: Asset deals and share deals
body: In a share deal the buyer acquires the company with all its history: contracts, licences, staff and hidden liabilities such as old tax assessments. In an asset deal the buyer picks the assets and liabilities it wants, leaving the rest behind, but each asset must be transferred separately: land use rights, vehicles, licences and contracts may each need consents and re-registration.

In Ethiopia, licences are often personal to the company, which favours share deals for regulated businesses such as banks, insurers and exporters with established quotas. Asset deals suit carve-outs and privatisations of a single plant. Tax differs: a share sale may produce a capital gain for the seller under the Income Tax Proclamation No. 979/2016 as amended, while an asset sale can bring VAT and transfer costs on individual assets. Obtain tax advice on each structure before setting the price.

left.title: Share deal
items: Buyer takes the whole company and its history
Licences and contracts usually stay in place
Seller may face capital gains tax on shares

right.title: Asset deal
items: VAT and transfer costs on individual assets

example.title: Buying the plant, not the company
example.text: A food group wanted the modern biscuit line of Adama Food Complex PLC but not its old tax dispute or the unprofitable bakery shops. It bought the factory building, the line and the brand as assets for ETB 310 million and hired the line staff on new contracts. The deal took four months longer than a share purchase because each asset had to be transferred, but the buyer left ETB 45 million of contested tax behind.

lessons.title: Cash, shares, deferred payment and earn-outs
body: Consideration can be cash, the buyer's shares, or a mix. Cash gives the seller certainty; shares let the seller share the upside and spare the buyer's cash, but they dilute existing owners. Deferred payment and vendor finance help a buyer that cannot raise the full amount at Ethiopian borrowing rates, while an earn-out pays part of the price only if the business hits agreed targets after closing.

Earn-outs bridge a gap in expectations, often in family business sales where the owners believe in growth the buyer will not pay for upfront. They work only with clear definitions: which accounts, which accounting policies, who controls the business during the earn-out period, and what happens if the buyer merges it into another unit. An escrow, a share of the price held by a third party for a set period, secures the seller's warranty and indemnity obligations.

worked.title: Guji Highland Coffee: consideration package for 60% (ETB millions)

rows.label: Escrow held 18 months for warranty claims (10% of headline)
Earn-out: 50% of year-2 EBITDA above ETB 120 million, capped at ETB 150 million
If year-2 EBITDA is ETB 170 million: earn-out 50% x 50
Total paid if EBITDA is ETB 170 million and no claims (560 + 76 + 124 + 25)

worked.note: The structure gives the family most of the price at closing, protects the buyer with escrow, and pays extra only for proven growth.

scenario.title: An earn-out the seller cannot control
scenario.situation: The buyer of Guji Highland Coffee proposes an earn-out on year-2 EBITDA but plans to move the company's export sales into its own trading arm in month six. The Tadesse siblings will stay on as managers.
scenario.question: What should the sellers' adviser insist on?
options: Accept: the buyer will act in good faith
Define earn-out EBITDA on a stand-alone basis with fixed accounting policies, require the business to be run separately during the period, and set a payout if the buyer integrates it early
Ask for the earn-out to be paid in advance
Drop the earn-out and accept ETB 640 million
scenario.explain: If the buyer can move sales elsewhere, it controls whether the target is met. Clear definitions, operating covenants and an acceleration payment protect the sellers.

lessons.title: Locked box or completion accounts
body: Price is usually agreed as an enterprise value, then converted to an equity price by deducting net debt and adjusting for working capital. With completion accounts, the parties draw up accounts at closing and adjust the price for actual net debt and working capital against a target. With a locked box, the price is fixed on a past balance sheet and the seller promises that no value has leaked out since then, such as dividends, bonuses or related-party payments.

A locked box gives price certainty and a simpler closing, but it needs reliable recent audited accounts and a strong no-leakage clause. Completion accounts protect the buyer when records are weaker, as they often are in Ethiopian family businesses, at the cost of post-closing disputes over the numbers. Many deals use completion accounts with an expert determination clause naming an independent audit firm to settle disagreements.

worked.title: Completion accounts: from enterprise value to equity price (ETB millions)

rows.label: Less net debt at completion (bank loans 230 minus cash 50)

worked.note: Every birr of extra net debt reduces the price; every birr of working capital above the target increases it.

example.title: Leakage after the locked box date
example.text: The buyer of a fictional Mekelle construction materials company agreed a locked box price on 30 June accounts. Due diligence later found that the owners had paid themselves ETB 18 million in 'consultancy fees' in August. Because the SPA defined leakage to include payments to sellers and their relatives, the buyer recovered the full amount birr for birr before closing.

lessons.title: Term sheet, SPA, warranties and indemnities
body: The term sheet records the main commercial points: parties, structure, price and adjustments, consideration, key conditions, exclusivity and timetable. It is mostly non-binding, except for confidentiality, exclusivity and costs. The SPA turns it into binding obligations and allocates risk through representations and warranties (statements of fact about the target), indemnities (promises to pay birr for birr for specific known risks) and limitations (caps, thresholds and time limits on claims).

Conditions precedent list what must happen before closing: regulatory approvals, shareholder resolutions, third-party consents. A material adverse change (MAC) clause lets the buyer walk away if the target suffers a serious deterioration between signing and closing. In Ethiopia, long approval periods make the MAC definition important: should a large currency depreciation count? Sellers usually exclude general market and economy-wide events, and buyers seek to include events that hit the target disproportionately.

items.label: Warranties
items.text: Statements of fact: accounts, tax, title, litigation, compliance

items.label: Indemnities
items.text: Birr-for-birr cover for a known risk, such as a tax dispute

items.label: Limitations
items.text: Caps, de minimis thresholds and time limits on claims

items.label: Conditions precedent
items.text: NBE, competition and shareholder approvals before closing

items.label: MAC clause
items.text: Buyer's exit if the target suffers a serious adverse change

scenario.title: A known tax dispute
scenario.situation: Due diligence on Guji Highland Coffee finds an ETB 32 million tax assessment from 2022 under appeal. The sellers say the general tax warranty already covers it.
scenario.question: What protection should the buyer seek?
options: Rely on the general tax warranty
A price cut of ETB 1 million
A specific indemnity for the 2022 assessment, secured on the escrow, outside the general cap and threshold
No protection: the appeal may succeed
scenario.explain: A matter disclosed in diligence is usually carved out of warranty claims. A specific indemnity, backed by escrow, makes the sellers pay if the assessment is confirmed.

lessons.title: Shareholder agreements and minority governance
body: When a buyer takes less than full ownership, the shareholder agreement governs the relationship. Its core terms are board composition and appointment rights, reserved matters that need the minority's consent (budgets, new debt, dividends, related-party deals, issuing shares), information rights, transfer restrictions (pre-emption, right of first refusal), tag-along and drag-along rights, deadlock resolution and exit routes, including a possible listing on the Ethiopian Securities Exchange.

For a foreign strategic investor in a domestic bank capped at 40%, the shareholder agreement is how influence is earned, and it must sit within the bank governance rules. SBB/91/2024 requires at least nine directors, one-third independent, one-third elected by non-influential shareholders and at least two women, and caps proxy voting at 10% of subscribed capital. Board seat promises must therefore be designed around those blocks, not against them.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/91/2024, Bank corporate governance
regulation.text: Banks must have at least nine directors: one-third elected by non-influential shareholders, one-third by all shareholders and one-third independent, with at least two women. A shareholder with 2% or more is an influential shareholder. Terms last up to three years and no director may serve more than six consecutive years. Proxy voting is capped at 10% of subscribed capital.

example.title: Board rights within the rules
example.text: A fictional Kenyan bank negotiating a 30% stake in an Ethiopian bank asked for five of nine board seats. Its advisers redesigned the request: two seats elected by all shareholders using its voting weight, a right to nominate a candidate for chief risk officer subject to NBE approval, and reserved matters on capital raising and strategy. The investor gained real influence within SBB/91/2024 and the 40% cap.

lessons.title: Financing the price in Ethiopian conditions
body: Acquisition finance is constrained in Ethiopia. Bank lending to a single borrower group is limited to 25% of the lender's total capital under SBB/87/2024, a bank's own equity investments in non-bank businesses are capped under SBB/92/2024, and lending rates are high. A foreign acquirer bringing offshore debt faces the FXD/01/2024 external loan rules, including a 60:40 debt to equity cap for foreign investors, and must match USD debt service against birr cash flows.

So Ethiopian deals lean on equity, share consideration, vendor finance and earn-outs rather than heavy leverage. Dividend repatriation for foreign owners now runs through banks: FXD/04/2026 lets banks approve dividend and profit remittances without prior NBE approval, with monthly reporting, which makes foreign returns more predictable.

regulation.source: NBE Directive No. SBB/92/2024, Limits on bank investments
regulation.text: A bank may invest up to 5% in a single insurer, 10% in any other single non-bank business, and 15% of total capital in all non-bank equity together, with a 10% limit for real estate; it may own up to 100% of a capital market service provider with NBE approval. A bank cannot buy control of an ordinary company as an investment.

scenario.title: Can the bank fund the buyer?
scenario.situation: Ras Logistics PLC asks Bank D for an ETB 2.5 billion loan to buy a competitor. Bank D's total capital is ETB 8.7 billion and it already lends ETB 0.4 billion to Ras Logistics' group.
scenario.question: What is the main constraint?
options: The combined exposure of ETB 2.9 billion is 33% of total capital, above the 25% single-group limit of SBB/87/2024, so the bank must reduce, syndicate or restructure the request
The bank must buy shares instead
scenario.explain: SBB/87/2024 limits exposure to one counterparty group to 25% of total capital, here about ETB 2.2 billion. More equity, vendor finance or syndication is needed.

takeaways: Share deals keep licences and history; asset deals leave liabilities behind but need each asset transferred
Mix cash, shares, deferred payment, earn-outs and escrow to bridge price gaps and secure warranties
Locked box suits reliable accounts; completion accounts protect buyers where records are weak
Use specific indemnities for risks found in diligence and define the MAC clause with care
Shareholder agreements must work within SBB/91/2024, the foreign caps and the bank lending limits

quiz.q: Which structure usually keeps a bank or insurer's licence in place?
quiz.explain: In a share deal the licensed company itself is bought, so its licence normally continues.

quiz.q: Enterprise value is ETB 800 million, net debt ETB 150 million and working capital is ETB 10 million below target. Equity price is:
quiz.explain: 800 minus 150 minus 10 = 640.

quiz.q: What does a locked box structure rely on most?
options: Completion accounts drawn up at closing
Reliable past accounts and a strong no-leakage clause
quiz.explain: The price is fixed on past accounts, so the buyer depends on the no-leakage promise.

quiz.q: A risk found during due diligence is best covered by:
quiz.explain: Disclosed matters are usually excluded from warranty claims, so a specific indemnity is needed.

quiz.q: Under SBB/91/2024, what share of a bank's directors must be independent?
quiz.explain: One-third independent, one-third elected by non-influential shareholders and one-third by all shareholders.

quiz.q: Under FXD/04/2026, who approves a foreign shareholder's dividend remittance?
options: The bank, with monthly reporting to the NBE
quiz.explain: FXD/04/2026 lets banks approve dividend and profit remittances without prior NBE approval.

modules.title: Bank mergers in Ethiopia, integration and the merger simulation
modules.summary: Take the Bank A and Bank D merger through regulatory and shareholder approval, test capital, exposures and governance after the merger, plan the first 100 days and track synergy delivery.
objectives: Plan the regulatory and shareholder approval path for a merger of widely held Ethiopian banks
Test the merged bank's capital ratios, large exposures and governance against NBE directives
Negotiate exchange ratio, board composition and name as a package
Build a 100-day integration plan covering culture, systems migration and customer retention
Measure synergy delivery and act when it falls behind

lessons.title: The regulatory and shareholder path
body: No dedicated NBE bank merger directive was confirmed in the materials behind this course, so teams should agree the process with the NBE early and check for new guidance issued after the June 2026 capital deadline. In practice the path combines the Banking Business Proclamation No. 1360/2025 powers, the significant influence rules of SBB/89/2024, the governance rules of SBB/91/2024, competition clearance and the Commercial Code's merger steps.

Ethiopian private banks are widely held, often by thousands of shareholders. Each bank needs an extraordinary general meeting to approve the merger agreement, the exchange ratio and the new articles. Shareholder communication must start early: town halls, a clear explanation of the exchange ratio, and a plan for shareholders who will cross the 2% threshold. Creditors and depositors must be informed as the Commercial Code requires, and the merger is registered once all approvals are in hand.

items.label: Month 1
items.text: Heads of terms, informal NBE consultation, shareholder map

items.label: Months 2 to 3
items.text: Mutual due diligence, exchange ratio, draft merger agreement

items.label: Month 3
items.text: Boards approve; competition filing; NBE application

items.label: Months 4 to 5
items.text: EGMs of both banks; 2% holders and new directors submitted for NBE approval

items.label: Month 6
items.text: Final NBE approval, registration, legal day one

items.label: Day 1 to Day 100
items.text: Integration plan executed: brand, systems, branches, people

regulation.source: Banking Business Proclamation No. 1360/2025 and Commercial Code Proclamation No. 1243/2021
regulation.text: The Banking Business Proclamation gives the NBE licensing and prudential powers over banks, including changes in ownership. The Commercial Code governs mergers and amalgamations of share companies, share transfers and minority protection, and requires the merger to be approved by each company's general meeting with protection for creditors. Check the current texts for timelines and voting thresholds before planning dates.

scenario.title: A quorum problem
scenario.situation: Bank A has 11,400 shareholders, many of them diaspora holders with small stakes. At the first EGM call, attendance in person and by proxy reaches too few shares for a quorum, and one shareholder group arrives with proxies for 14% of subscribed capital.
scenario.question: What should Bank A's team do?
options: Reject proxies above the 10% cap, adjourn, and run a structured outreach campaign before the reconvened meeting
Count the 14% proxy block to reach the quorum
Hold the vote anyway and file later
Ask Bank D to vote Bank A's shares
scenario.explain: SBB/91/2024 caps proxy voting at 10% of subscribed capital. A failed quorum calls for adjournment and active outreach, not shortcuts that would make the resolution open to challenge.

lessons.title: Capital, exposures and related parties after the merger
body: The merged bank must meet every prudential limit from legal day one. Combine the two banks' capital and risk-weighted assets, deduct goodwill and intangibles from CET1 as the capital directive requires, and test CET1, Tier 1 and total capital against 7%, 9% and 11%. Then aggregate exposures to the same borrower groups across both loan books: two exposures that were each within 25% of each bank's capital can breach the limit together.

Related parties change too. Shareholders of Bank A who become 2% holders of the merged bank, and their companies, become related parties, and the 15% single and 35% aggregate related-party limits of SBB/88/2024 apply to the combined book. These tests belong in due diligence, not after closing.

worked.title: Merged bank: capital and a large exposure test (ETB billions)

rows.label: Less goodwill from the purchase price allocation
Total capital ratio after goodwill deduction (12.47 / 86.7)
Exposure to Hamle Construction group: A 1.1 + D 2.2
Exposure as share of merged capital (3.3 / 12.47)
Reduction needed to reach 25% (3.3 minus 0.25 x 12.47)

worked.note: The merger strengthens capital but creates a large exposure breach; agree a reduction or participation plan with the borrower before legal day one.

regulation.source: NBE Directives No. SBB/87/2024 and SBB/88/2024, Large exposures and related party transactions
regulation.text: Exposure to one counterparty group may not exceed 25% of total capital, and an exposure of 10% or more is a large exposure reported monthly within 20 days. Exposure to a single related party is limited to 15% and to all related parties to 35%, on arm's length terms, with board approval above Birr 15 million.

lessons.title: Exchange ratio, board and name as one package
body: In the merger simulation, teams negotiate three items that are linked: the exchange ratio, board composition and the name of the merged bank. Treating them separately leads to deadlock. Treating them as a package lets each side trade: Bank A's side may accept the book value ratio of 0.902 in return for three board seats it nominates and a name that keeps its brand in the regions where it is strong.

Board composition must fit SBB/91/2024. With nine directors, three are independent, three are elected by non-influential shareholders and three by all shareholders. At 34.6% ownership, Bank A's former shareholders can expect to influence about a third of the elected seats; promising more cannot be guaranteed because directors are elected, not appointed. The chair, the CEO and the chief risk officer are separate decisions, and the CEO and senior executives need NBE approval under SBB/89/2024.

scenario.title: Deadlock on the name
scenario.situation: In the simulation, Bank A's team insists the merged bank keep Bank A's name; Bank D's team refuses because Bank D's shareholders will own 65.4%. Talks have stalled for two rounds and the capital deadline has already passed for Bank A.
scenario.question: Which move is most likely to break the deadlock?
options: Bank A's team threatens to walk away
Ask the NBE to choose the name
Offer a package: Bank D's name for the legal entity, Bank A's brand kept for its regional branches for three years, and Bank A nominating the deputy chair, in exchange for accepting the 0.902 ratio
scenario.explain: Linking the name to the ratio and governance lets each side give where it cares less. Bank A, which needs the deal more, gains brand continuity and a visible role without forcing a higher ratio.

lessons.title: The 100-day integration plan
body: Integration starts before closing. An integration management office, led by a senior executive from each bank, owns a plan with workstreams for people, branches, products and pricing, IT and data, risk and compliance, finance and reporting, and communication. The first 100 days set the tone: decide the top two levels of management quickly, keep key relationship managers, and tell staff, customers and shareholders what will change and when.

Systems migration is the riskiest workstream. Running two core banking systems for a time is normal, but the migration to one platform must be rehearsed with mock conversions and reconciliations, and scheduled away from peak periods such as month-end payroll or holidays. Culture work is as concrete as IT: common credit approval limits, one service standard, and visible early decisions that are fair to both sides.

items.label: Before closing
items.text: Integration office, workstream leads, day one checklist

items.label: Day 1
items.text: Legal merger, new board and CEO, messages to staff and customers

items.label: Days 1 to 30
items.text: Top two management levels named, retention of key staff, unchanged service

items.label: Days 30 to 60
items.text: Common credit and risk policies, product and pricing map

items.label: Days 60 to 100
items.text: Branch overlap plan, migration rehearsal, first synergy report

example.title: The weekend migration that waited
example.text: Two fictional microfinance institutions merging in Tigray planned to move to one core system over a holiday weekend. A mock conversion two weeks earlier found that 4% of savings accounts failed to reconcile because of different interest accrual methods. The team delayed the cutover by six weeks, fixed the mapping and ran a second rehearsal. Customers saw no errors on go-live, which mattered more than the six weeks.

lessons.tip: Name the top two levels of management within 30 days; uncertainty is when good staff leave.

lessons.title: Keeping customers, staff and deposits
body: Deposits are the main funding of Ethiopian banks, and they can walk. During a merger, competitors approach the best customers and relationship managers. Retention starts with a list: the top depositors, borrowers and trade finance clients of both banks, each with a named owner who calls them before the announcement reaches the market. Keep account numbers, cards and mobile banking working without change for as long as possible.

Staff rationalisation must be planned with care and in line with Ethiopian labour law: identify overlapping roles, offer redeployment to new branches or functions first, and apply clear, fair selection criteria. Branch closures should follow customer data, not seniority: keep the branch with more deposits and better access, and move staff and customers together.

scenario.title: Closing the overlapping branch
scenario.situation: In Bahir Dar, Bank A's branch holds ETB 1.9 billion of deposits and Bank D's branch, 300 metres away, holds ETB 0.7 billion. Bank D's regional manager wants to keep Bank D's branch because it is newer and he is senior.
scenario.question: Which branch should the integration team keep?
options: Bank D's, because the merged bank carries Bank D's name
Bank A's, because it holds most of the deposits, while moving Bank D's customers and staff into it with a named relationship plan
Neither: close both and open a new one
scenario.explain: Customer value, not seniority, should decide. Keeping the branch with ETB 1.9 billion and moving the smaller one's customers with care protects deposits and delivers the cost saving.

lessons.title: Measuring synergy delivery
body: Synergies promised to the board and the NBE must be tracked like a budget. Each synergy has an owner, a baseline, a target by quarter and a measure that finance can verify, such as the actual rent and staff cost of closed branches. Track one-off costs against their budget too, and report deposit attrition, because a cost saving that loses deposits may destroy value.

Advanced practice is to report net synergies, benefits minus costs minus leakage, every quarter to the board, with a traffic light for each line. When a line falls behind, ask whether the problem is timing, which can be recovered, or a flawed assumption, which must be written down and reflected in the plan.

worked.title: Merged bank: synergy tracker at month 12 (ETB millions, annualised)

rows.label: Branch closures: target 147 by month 12 (70% of 210) / actual
Core banking: target 30 / actual (migration slipped one quarter)
Integration cost to date: budget 300 / actual

worked.note: Head office savings are ahead, but migration delay and higher attrition mean the year 2 plan should be reset and a customer retention push launched in the overlapping cities.

example.title: Learning from an African bank merger
example.text: For the applied assignment, learners analyse a real African bank merger from public sources: the rationale, the exchange ratio or price, approvals, what happened to market share, staff and costs in the following years, and what the deal teaches for Ethiopia. Cases where synergies were tracked publicly, and where they were not, make the best comparisons.

lessons.title: Capstone: the merger simulation and integration plan
body: The capstone is a negotiated merger of Bank A and Bank D. Teams are split into Bank A and Bank D sides, each with confidential instructions: Bank A's side must close to meet the capital rule, Bank D's side has a walk-away exchange ratio and a minimum share of board influence. They negotiate the exchange ratio, board composition and name as a package, then together present the merged bank's integration plan.

The integration plan covers the regulatory path and timetable, merged capital ratios and any limit breaches with fixes, the governance structure under SBB/91/2024, the 100-day plan, the branch and staff plan, the customer retention plan and the synergy tracker. Assessment weights follow the course specification: simulation and integration plan 40%, test 30%, applied case analysis of a real African bank merger 20% and participation 10%.
points: Exchange ratio with the value transfer explained
Board composition that fits SBB/91/2024
Name and brand decision and its rationale
Merged capital ratios after goodwill and exposure tests
100-day plan, branch and staff plan, retention plan
Synergy targets, owners and the quarterly tracker

takeaways: Agree the bank merger path with the NBE early; no dedicated merger directive was confirmed
Widely held banks need shareholder outreach, a 2% holder map and respect for the 10% proxy cap
Test merged capital after goodwill, aggregate large exposures and new related parties before legal day one
Negotiate ratio, board and name as one package within SBB/91/2024
Run integration through a 100-day plan and track net synergies, costs and deposit attrition every quarter

quiz.q: Two exposures to the same group, ETB 1.1 billion and ETB 2.2 billion, are combined in a merged bank with ETB 12.47 billion of capital. The exposure is:
quiz.explain: 3.3 / 12.47 = 26.5%, above the SBB/87/2024 limit of 25% of total capital.

quiz.q: What is the cap on proxy voting under SBB/91/2024?
quiz.explain: SBB/91/2024 caps proxy voting at 10% of subscribed capital.

quiz.q: Which workstream usually carries the highest operational risk in a bank merger?
quiz.explain: Data conversion and reconciliation errors can disrupt every customer, so migration needs rehearsal.

quiz.q: Synergies delivered are ETB 167 million against a target of ETB 212 million. Delivery is about:
Why negotiate exchange ratio, board and name as a package?
options: Because the NBE requires one document
So each side can trade items it values less for items it values more
Because the name sets the ratio
quiz.explain: Linking items allows trades and avoids deadlock on any single point.

quiz.q: Which test belongs in due diligence before a bank merger closes?
options: Aggregated large exposures and related-party limits on the combined book
quiz.explain: Breaches of SBB/87/2024 or SBB/88/2024 must be found and fixed before legal day one.

exam.q: A beverage maker buys its main bottle supplier mainly to secure supply and quality. Which statement is best?
options: It is horizontal and justified by scale
It is conglomerate and needs no synergies
It is vertical; the case rests on supply security and margin, which must outweigh the premium and integration cost
exam.explain: A supplier sits upstream in the same chain, and the deal creates value only if those benefits exceed premium and integration cost.

exam.q: A domestic bank wants a foreign strategic partner. Which offer can be accepted as structured?
options: A foreign strategic investor buys 35% with board nomination rights
Three related foreign companies buy 20% each
exam.explain: SBB/94/2025 allows a strategic investor up to 40%; 51% breaches it, related companies would be treated together, and an individual is capped at 7%.

exam.q: Bank E has a total capital ratio of 11.4%. Bank A, at 13.9%, is a third of its size. Why is Bank E still a weak partner for Bank A?
options: Its thin margin over the 11% minimum leaves little room for goodwill deductions and integration losses
SBB/95/2025 does not apply to it
exam.explain: A merged ratio near 11% after goodwill and fair value adjustments could fall below the minimum.

exam.q: Buyer EPS is Birr 300. Combined profit is ETB 3,600 million and combined shares are 12.5 million. The deal is:
exam.explain: Combined EPS is 3,600 / 12.5 = Birr 288, which is 4% below Birr 300.

exam.q: In the Bank A and Bank D case, after-tax synergies needed to break even are about ETB 217 million. Expected after-tax run-rate synergies are ETB 210 million. What should the board conclude?
options: The exchange ratio should be raised
Even with full synergies the deal is slightly dilutive at the book value ratio, so any premium to Bank A must be traded for value
exam.explain: Full synergies leave EPS 0.3% below stand-alone; a premium would deepen the dilution.

exam.q: Price paid is ETB 5,520 million and fair value of net identifiable assets is ETB 4,691 million. If goodwill is deducted from CET1, how much capital is excluded?
exam.explain: Goodwill is 5,520 minus 4,691 = ETB 829 million, which reduces counted CET1.

exam.q: Which approval sequence is most sensible for a bank merger?
options: EGMs, then NBE, then competition check
Informal NBE consultation and competition check, boards, NBE application, EGMs, then final approvals and registration
exam.explain: Early consultation avoids asking shareholders to approve terms the regulator may reject.

exam.q: A family business sale has three credible but cautious bidders. Which process fits best?
options: A public auction with a newspaper advertisement
A hybrid: confidential approaches under NDAs, then a short competitive second round
exam.explain: A hybrid keeps confidentiality while still creating competitive tension.

exam.q: A bidder demands exclusivity ten days before binding bids are due, offering a slightly higher non-binding number. The seller's adviser should usually:
options: Keep the timetable and ask for the best binding offer by the deadline
exam.explain: Exclusivity gives up competitive tension; it should follow, not precede, binding offers.

exam.q: Synergies have a run-rate of ETB 300 million pre-tax, but integration costs fall in years 1 and 2 and full benefits only from year 3. At a 22% discount rate their present value was about ETB 550 million. What does this show?
options: Synergies are worth ten times run-rate
Run-rate multiples overstate value when costs come first and benefits later
exam.explain: Phasing and high Ethiopian discount rates cut synergy value well below simple multiples.

exam.q: Target stand-alone value is ETB 1,400 million and net synergies are worth ETB 300 million. The seller's best alternative is ETB 1,500 million. The negotiating range is:
exam.explain: The seller's floor is its best alternative and the buyer's ceiling is stand-alone value plus synergies.

exam.q: Bank A's holders receive 0.31 million extra Bank D shares from a 10% exchange ratio premium, at Birr 1,800 each. Compared with the ETB 550 million PV of synergies, this premium:
options: Transfers about all synergy value to Bank A's holders
exam.explain: 0.31 million x 1,800 is about ETB 552 million, close to the full PV of synergies.

exam.q: Which situation favours an asset deal over a share deal?
options: Buying one plant while leaving behind a contested tax liability and loss-making shops
Buying a company whose export quota is tied to the company
exam.explain: An asset deal lets the buyer leave unwanted liabilities behind, at the cost of transferring each asset.

exam.q: An earn-out pays 40% of year-2 EBITDA above ETB 200 million, capped at ETB 60 million. Year-2 EBITDA is ETB 260 million. The earn-out payment is:
exam.explain: 40% x (260 minus 200) = ETB 24 million, below the cap.

exam.q: Enterprise value is ETB 1,000 million, net debt at completion ETB 220 million, and working capital is ETB 15 million above target. The equity price is:
exam.explain: 1,000 minus 220 plus 15 = ETB 795 million.

exam.q: Between signing and closing, a large birr depreciation hits all importers. The target is an importer hit no worse than its peers. Under a typical seller-friendly MAC clause:
options: The buyer probably cannot walk away, because economy-wide events affecting the target no more than peers are usually excluded
exam.explain: Sellers usually exclude general market and economic events unless the target is hit disproportionately.

exam.q: A lender's total capital is ETB 10 billion and it already lends ETB 0.8 billion to a group seeking acquisition finance. Under SBB/87/2024 the most it can add is about:
exam.explain: The group limit is 25% of ETB 10 billion = ETB 2.5 billion, less ETB 0.8 billion already lent.

exam.q: A foreign investor with 30% of a domestic bank asks to appoint five of nine directors. The best adviser response is:
options: Explain that SBB/91/2024 fixes thirds for independent, non-influential and all-shareholder seats, and design influence through elected seats, reserved matters and nomination rights
Reduce the board to five members
exam.explain: Board seat promises must fit the SBB/91/2024 composition, and directors are elected, so influence comes from structure and rights.

exam.q: Twelve months after merger, net synergies are behind plan because migration slipped a quarter, while deposit attrition is ETB 34 million against ETB 20 million assumed. The best response is:
options: Separate timing from flawed assumptions, reset the year 2 plan and launch a targeted retention push
Close more branches immediately to catch up
exam.explain: Migration delay is timing; higher attrition suggests a flawed assumption that needs action and a revised plan.

exam.q: Bank A's branch holds ETB 1.9 billion of deposits and Bank D's nearby branch ETB 0.7 billion. Bank D's manager is more senior. Which branch should stay open?
options: Bank A's, with Bank D's customers and staff moved under a named retention plan
Bank D's, because its manager is senior
exam.explain: Customer value decides; keep the branch with most deposits and move the other's customers with care.

sources: Erudite Africa course specification 3.c: Mergers and Acquisitions (M&A) Strategy and Execution, Levels 1 and 2 (October 2026)
Erudite Africa Training Module: Ethiopian Context, programme overview and regulatory register (October 2026)
NBE directives as listed in the lessons: SBB/78/2021 (reported), SBB/87/2024, SBB/88/2024, SBB/89/2024, SBB/91/2024, SBB/92/2024, SBB/94/2025, SBB/95/2025, MFI/36/2023, FXD/01/2024 and FXD/04/2026

Banking Business Proclamation No. 1360/2025; Investment Proclamation No. 1180/2020 and Investment Board Directive No. 1082/2025; Income Tax Proclamation No. 979/2016 as amended by No. 1395/2025; Capital Market Proclamation No. 1248/2021 and ECMA Directive No. 980/2024
Commercial Code Proclamation No. 1243/2021 and the Trade Competition and Consumers Protection Proclamation No. 813/2013, as cited in the course specification (texts to be checked)
General M&A market practice on process, valuation, SPA terms and integration; all companies and people in examples are fictional
